chunks: Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhal narrated from Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Hakim from Jamil ibn Darraj from Abu Abdillah and Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon them) that they said:

"There is no zakat on raw gold (tibra); rather, it is upon the dinars and dirhams." And it is considered that, in addition to being struck (minted), they must be engraved/inscribed, because that which is not engraved follows the ruling of the ingot (sibakah) and the nugget (niqar).

key_terms.التِّبْرِ: Raw gold or gold in its natural, uncoined state
key_terms.النِّقَارِ: Nuggets or small lumps of gold
key_terms.مَنْقُوشَةً: Engraved or inscribed (referring to the markings on coins)

ai.seo_question: What is the condition for gold coins to be subject to zakat according to this hadith?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the distinction between raw gold (tibra) and coined currency (dinar/dirham) for zakat, a key issue in early Shia jurisprudence regarding the definition of 'nisab' and 'hawl'. The condition of being 'manqusha' (engraved/inscribed) ensures the gold functions as recognized currency rather than bullion, reflecting the economic context of the Abbasid era where coinage standards varied. This ruling underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on the functional status of wealth in determining zakat liability.
